summary:
Portugal remains among the safer European destinations for transgender visitors. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is lawful, and legal gender and name change currently runs under the 2018 self-determination law, which allows self-declaration from age 16 without a medical requirement. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, conversion therapy has been banned since 2024, surgical intervention on intersex infants is prohibited, and access to facilities matching a person's gender is protected.

The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offending. Under Articles 132, 144 and 145, an offence determined by hatred on those grounds is aggravated, with aggravated assault punishable by up to four years, and organising discrimination on those grounds carrying penalties of one to eight years.

That baseline is under active legislative pressure. On 19 and 20 March 2026 the Assembleia da República debated and approved three bills tabled by the PSD, Chega and CDS-PP, the first parliamentary vote to roll back self-identification in legal gender recognition. The proposals passed by 124 votes to 79 and were referred to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees. At first reading Parliament backed reinstating a mandatory medical opinion for any change of legal gender and name, undoing the 2018 reform.

As recorded in the sources, the bills have cleared only their first reading and have not been enacted, so the 2018 framework remains the operative law for legal gender and name change. The package also puts the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children in question. A European Parliament written question, E-001183/2026, put the health and safety of transgender people in Portugal and the repeal process to the Commission. Nothing in the record indicates criminalisation of trans people or any restriction on their entry or presence in the country.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th on 67%, one place down, with no affirmative legislation adopted since the 2024 ban on conversion practices. The score sits below Malta, Iceland and Belgium but above most of the continent. The joint statement by IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warned that adoption of the three bills would cost Portugal at least four further places, dropping it below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France and ending its standing as a regional reference point.

The political contest is unusually open. The Ordem dos Psicólogos and trans organisations described the bills as a retrocesso, while socialist deputies invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in Porto, against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Forbidden Colours called the vote a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

Public opinion runs against the legislative direction. Equaldex records high public support for same-sex parenting in Portugal, ranked first among 30 EU regions, alongside its ratings of legal homosexuality, marriage, unrestricted gender change, lawful gender-affirming care, the intersex surgery ban, hate-crime coverage, the discrimination ban, the conversion-therapy ban and protected bathroom access.
localsOnly:
Justice Ministry figures show legal sex and name changes climbing back toward the high-water mark recorded two years earlier, with the largest number in Lisbon, an uptick registered while Parliament advances the bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 law scrapped.

Committee-stage analysis by the Comissão para a Cidadania e a Igualdade de Género warned that the bills worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people, defended the existing duties of schools to prevent discrimination, and assessed the Bloco de Esquerda bill as compatible with schools' human-rights obligations.

The Provedor de Justiça has requested a constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, the provision establishing the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, with the institutional watchdog questioning the hate-speech provision itself.
outOfScopeNotes:
The final outcome of the three bills is unresolved in the sources: only the first reading of 20 March 2026 and the referral to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees are documented, and no source records a final vote, promulgation or entry into force.

Whether the 2018 self-determination law's provisions, including self-declaration from age 16, and the prohibition on surgical intervention on intersex infants survive the package is not sourced. Nor is the fate of the Provedor de Justiça's request for constitutional review of Article 176-C.

Entry, visa and document-screening practice for transgender visitors, including how foreign passport gender markers are handled at the border, is not covered by the inventory. Enforcement rates for the Penal Code's hate-crime aggravation and for the discrimination ban are likewise not sourced here.
